title: Delta tables: files, log, and snapshots
summary: Predict committed table rows from a schematic file/log timeline and separate storage correctness from business correctness.
objectives: Predict committed table rows from a schematic file/log timeline and separate storage correctness from business correctness.
Apply the reasoning to a changed case and explain the limits of the evidence.

sections.title: Files are physical; a snapshot is logical

questions.prompt: What does a successful transactional table write fail to prove?

options.text: That the source’s business meaning and values are correct.
options.rationale: Atomic table behavior does not validate every business rule.

options.text: That a table update can be committed.
options.rationale: The successful write is evidence of that narrow operation.

options.text: That the source record was supplied to the write.
options.rationale: The operation used its supplied input, but that input may be wrong.

questions.prompt: An external reader fails after a table feature change. What should be checked first?

options.rationale: A fresh cache cannot give an incompatible reader support for a newly required table feature.
More time does not resolve an unsupported reader protocol.
A feature can impose requirements on participating clients.

questions.prompt: File f0 remains physically present after version 1 retired it. What belongs in a version 1 table read?

options.text: Only rows active in the committed version 1 snapshot.
options.rationale: Physical presence does not make a file logically current.

options.text: Every row in f0, f1 and f2.
options.rationale: That bypasses the table log and double-counts A.

options.text: Whichever file has the latest filesystem modification time.
options.rationale: Filesystem arrival time does not define the committed table snapshot.

questions.prompt: What happens if a replacement data file is written but its transaction never commits?

options.text: The old data is automatically proven invalid.
options.rationale: Failure to commit a new change says nothing about the business truth of the prior state.

options.text: That file alone does not establish a new committed table snapshot.
options.rationale: The transaction boundary determines the visible change.

options.text: The new row automatically becomes current because the bytes exist.
options.rationale: Physical writing is not the same as committing table metadata.

cards.prompt: What are storage, compute, table format, and governance responsible for?
cards.answer: Bytes, execution, table behavior, and permitted use respectively.
cards.explanation: Keep the responsibilities distinct when explaining an architecture.

cards.prompt: Why does ACID not mean business correctness?
cards.answer: A transaction can reliably commit values whose meaning or source is wrong.
cards.explanation: Source semantics and validation remain separate work: the transaction guarantees which state was committed, while business rules decide which records should have crossed that boundary at all.

cards.prompt: What must be checked before enabling a table feature?
cards.answer: Compatibility of every required reader and writer.
cards.explanation: A feature that helps one engine can affect other clients.

cards.prompt: Why does scanning every physical file differ from reading a Delta table?
cards.answer: The table snapshot includes only logically active data for its committed version.
cards.explanation: Old or uncommitted physical files are not automatically current rows.

cards.prompt: How do table version and source revision differ?
cards.answer: A table version identifies a commit; a source revision orders a business record’s changes.
cards.explanation: One table commit can contain many business revisions.

cards.prompt: A replacement file exists but its transaction never committed. What can a current reader infer?
cards.answer: Physical file creation alone does not establish a new committed table snapshot.
cards.explanation: The last committed snapshot remains the reading basis; investigate failed writes through supported APIs.

cards.prompt: After a commit replaces A0 (10 units) with A1 (12 units) beside unchanged C (8), what does the new snapshot total?
cards.answer: 20 inspected units: 12 replaces 10, so the total rises by 2, not by 12.
cards.explanation: A commit excludes A0 and includes A1 in one atomic membership change; there is no intermediate state with neither or both A files. A0’s bytes may still sit in the folder, but the snapshot no longer selects them, so counting both representations would give the wrong 30.

cards.prompt: A table’s history still lists version v0. Why might reading v0 fail anyway?
cards.answer: Time travel needs the retained data files and a permitted age; a visible history entry alone guarantees neither.
cards.explanation: Operation history, deleted-file retention and runtime age limits are three separate questions. If A0 was removed by retention cleanup, v0 cannot be reproduced and a result silently missing A0 is not a successful reproduction; raising the retention setting later cannot resurrect bytes already deleted.

cards.prompt: Row B1 = (-3, 1) matches the integer column types. Is the row therefore valid?
cards.answer: No. Schema enforcement checks structure; a negative inspected quantity breaks a domain rule that needs its own check.
cards.explanation: Structural, domain and cross-record checks rest on different evidence. Column names, types and nullability are the schema’s promise; nonnegative quantities, defective not exceeding inspected, and one payload per event identity are business rules enforced at the layer that actually holds that evidence, never by one green quality icon.

cards.prompt: Two writers replace the same file from one starting snapshot. What happens at the second commit?
cards.answer: Validation compares the second writer’s assumptions with the intervening commit; an overlapping change fails instead of silently corrupting the table.
cards.explanation: Optimistic concurrency separates preparation from acceptance: both writers can prepare work, but the later committer is checked against what changed meanwhile. Independent appends occupy a different cell of the documented conflict matrix, so the word concurrent alone does not predict failure, and a retry must re-read the latest state and re-apply the business ordering rule.
